title: Call parentheses
short: Runs the callable named just before it, passing whatever is between the parentheses as arguments.
long: The parentheses are what actually executes a function; the name on its own only refers to it. Whatever sits between them becomes the arguments. An empty pair still calls the function, just with no arguments.

title: Parameter list opener
short: Begins the list of parameters a function accepts, right after its name in a def statement.
long: Everything up to the matching ) names the inputs the function expects. This is a declaration, not a call, so no code runs here. An empty pair means the function takes no parameters.

title: Base class list opener
short: Begins the list of parent classes this class inherits from.
long: Names between the parentheses are superclasses; their attributes and methods are inherited. Leaving the parentheses off means the class inherits only from object.

title: Tuple grouping
short: Bounds a set of comma-separated values that together form one immutable tuple.
long: It is really the commas that build the tuple; the parentheses just delimit it and make it readable. A single-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (1,). The empty pair () is the one case that means an empty tuple by itself.

title: Generator expression
short: Wraps a lazy generator expression that yields values one at a time instead of building a collection.
long: It looks like a list comprehension but with parentheses, so nothing is materialised up front. Each value is computed only when consumed, which keeps memory flat for large sequences.
example: sum(x * x for x in nums)

title: Grouping parentheses
short: Groups a sub-expression so it is evaluated first, overriding normal operator precedence.
long: This creates no object; it only controls evaluation order and readability. It is also the clean way to spread a long expression across several lines without trailing backslashes.

title: Closing parenthesis
short: Closes the nearest open ( — ending an argument list, a parameter list, a tuple, or a grouped expression.
long: Every ( must be balanced by exactly one ). For a call or class definition, reaching this point is what triggers the call or builds the class.

title: List literal opener
short: Begins a list: an ordered, mutable sequence of the comma-separated values that follow.
long: The brackets themselves construct a new list object. An empty pair [] is a valid empty list. Items keep their insertion order and can be changed, added, or removed later.

title: Subscript / index bracket
short: Indexes into or slices the object immediately before it — a list, string, dict, or anything defining __getitem__.
long: What goes inside is a key, an integer index (negative counts from the end), or a slice. The object decides what the brackets mean, so the same syntax reads a list element, a dict value, or a DataFrame column.

title: List comprehension
short: Builds a new list by evaluating an expression once per item drawn from an iterable, optionally filtered.
long: It is a compact for-loop that collects results. Read it left to right: the output expression, then the for clause, then any if filter. The whole thing produces one finished list.
example: squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]

title: Closing bracket
short: Closes the nearest open [ — ending a list literal, an index/slice, or a list comprehension.
long: Every [ pairs with exactly one ]. For a subscript it marks where the index expression stops.

title: Dict literal opener
short: Begins a dictionary: a set of key: value pairs giving fast lookup by key.
long: The braces build a new dict object. Keys must be hashable and unique; assigning a duplicate key overwrites it. An empty pair {} is an empty dict, not an empty set.

title: Set literal opener
short: Begins a set: an unordered collection of unique, hashable values with no keys.
long: Written like a dict but with bare values and no colons. Duplicates are silently dropped. There is no empty-set literal — use set() for that, since {} means an empty dict.

title: Dict comprehension
short: Builds a dict by producing a key: value pair for each item taken from an iterable.
long: Same shape as a list comprehension but the output is 'key: value'. Later pairs with a repeated key win.

title: Set comprehension
short: Builds a set by evaluating one expression per item from an iterable, keeping only distinct results.
long: Like a list comprehension but wrapped in braces with a single output expression, so the result is a set with duplicates removed.

title: f-string replacement field
short: Opens a slot inside an f-string where the enclosed expression is evaluated and its result inserted.
long: Only valid inside a string with an f prefix. An optional !r/!s conversion and a :format-spec may follow the expression before the closing brace. To print a literal brace in an f-string, double it: {{ or }}.

title: Closing brace
short: Closes the nearest open { — ending a dict or set literal, a comprehension, or an f-string field.
long: Every { pairs with exactly one }. Inside an f-string it marks where the embedded expression ends.

title: Block colon
short: Ends a compound-statement header (def, class, if, for, while, with, try, else, except) and introduces its indented body.
long: Everything indented under the next lines belongs to this block. The colon is required even when the body is a single line written after it.

title: Type annotation colon
short: Separates a name from a type hint, on a variable or a function parameter.
long: The annotation is recorded but not enforced at runtime; it documents intent and helps type checkers and editors. A default value, if any, comes after the annotation with =.

title: Slice colon
short: Separates start, stop, and step inside square brackets to select a range rather than a single item.
long: The form is [start:stop:step]; any part may be omitted. stop is exclusive. A bare [:] copies the whole sequence.

title: Key/value colon
short: Binds a key to its value inside a dict literal or dict comprehension.
long: The expression on the left is the key (it must be hashable); the expression on the right is the stored value.

title: Lambda colon
short: Separates a lambda's parameter list from the single expression it returns.
long: A lambda has no block and no return statement; whatever follows the colon is evaluated and returned when the lambda is called.

title: Comma separator
short: Separates items in a list, tuple, set, dict, call, or parameter list.
long: In tuple context the comma is the operator that actually builds the tuple. A trailing comma before a closing bracket is legal and keeps diffs small.

title: Attribute access
short: Reaches into the object on its left to get the named attribute or method that follows.
long: Python looks the name up on the instance, then its class, then base classes. A trailing () after the name would then call the method it found.

title: Statement separator
short: Puts two simple statements on one physical line.
long: Rarely used in idiomatic Python, which prefers one statement per line. It cannot join compound statements such as def or if.

title: Ellipsis literal
short: The singleton Ellipsis object, most often used as a 'to be filled in' placeholder body.
long: In stub files and abstract methods it stands in for real code. NumPy also uses it inside subscripts to mean 'all remaining axes'.

title: Decorator
short: Wraps the function or class defined just below it with the callable named after the @.
long: def f... followed by @deco is shorthand for f = deco(f). Decorators add behaviour (caching, registration, access checks) without editing the function body. Multiple decorators apply bottom-up.

title: Matrix multiplication operator
short: Multiplies two operands using their __matmul__ method — matrix product for NumPy arrays.
long: Distinct from * which is element-wise. Plain Python numbers do not define it; it is meaningful mainly for array libraries.

title: Return type annotation
short: Introduces the hint for what a function returns, between the parameter list's ) and the block colon.
long: Like other annotations it is informational, not enforced. Use -> None for functions that return nothing useful.

title: Walrus / assignment expression
short: Assigns a value to a name and returns that value as part of a larger expression.
long: Lets you bind and test in one place, e.g. in a while condition or an if. Needs parentheses in many positions. Use sparingly — it can hurt readability.

title: Assignment
short: Binds the name on the left to the object produced by the expression on the right.
long: It does not copy; the name becomes another reference to the same object. Chained targets (a = b = 0) bind several names to one value.

title: Keyword argument
short: Passes an argument by parameter name inside a call: name=value.
long: No spaces around = by convention here. Keyword arguments may appear in any order and make call sites self-documenting.

title: Default parameter value
short: Gives a parameter a fallback value used when the caller omits it.
long: Evaluated once, when the def runs — so a mutable default like [] is shared across calls and is usually a bug. Prefer None plus a check inside.

title: Annotated assignment
short: Assigns a value on a line that also carries a type annotation after the name.
long: The form is name: Type = value. The annotation is stored in __annotations__; the = part does the actual binding.

title: Addition / concatenation
short: Adds numbers, or joins two sequences of the same kind (str+str, list+list).
long: The operands must be compatible: you cannot add a str and an int. For repeated joining of many strings, ''.join() is faster than chained +.

title: Unary plus
short: A no-op on ordinary numbers; kept for symmetry with unary minus and custom __pos__.
long: You will rarely write it. Some Decimal contexts use it to apply rounding, and custom classes may override __pos__.

title: Subtraction
short: Subtracts the right operand from the left; also set difference for two sets.
long: Works on all numeric types, mixing int and float by promoting to float.

title: Unary minus / negation
short: Negates the value that follows it.
long: Binds tighter than most binary operators, so -a ** 2 is -(a ** 2). Calls __neg__ on custom types.

title: Multiplication / repetition
short: Multiplies numbers, or repeats a sequence a whole number of times ("ab" * 3).
long: Sequence repetition shares references, so [ [] ] * 3 gives three views of the same inner list.

title: *args parameter
short: In a def, collects all extra positional arguments into one tuple.
long: A bare * with no name instead marks the start of keyword-only parameters. The conventional name is args.

title: Iterable unpacking
short: Spreads the items of an iterable into a call, a list/tuple literal, or an assignment target.
long: f(*xs) passes each element as its own argument; [*a, *b] concatenates; first, *rest = seq captures the remainder as a list.

title: Exponentiation
short: Raises the left operand to the power of the right.
long: Right-associative: 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 2 ** 9. A negative or fractional exponent yields a float (or complex).

title: **kwargs parameter
short: In a def, collects all extra keyword arguments into one dict.
long: The conventional name is kwargs. It must come last in the parameter list.

title: Mapping unpacking
short: Spreads a dict's key/value pairs into a call as keyword arguments or into another dict literal.
long: f(**opts) is the same as passing each key=value; {**a, **b} merges dicts, with b winning on shared keys.

title: True division
short: Divides and always produces a float, even when the result is whole.
long: 10 / 2 is 5.0, not 5. Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError.

title: Positional-only marker
short: In a def parameter list, everything before the / must be passed positionally, never by name.
long: Lets a library rename parameters later without breaking callers. Mirrors the * that starts keyword-only parameters.

title: Floor division
short: Divides and rounds the result down to the nearest whole number, toward negative infinity.
long: 7 // 2 is 3; -7 // 2 is -4. Returns an int when both operands are ints, otherwise a whole-valued float.

title: Modulo / remainder
short: Gives the remainder after floor division; the result takes the sign of the divisor.
long: Common uses: n % 2 to test even/odd, i % len to wrap an index. With a string on the left it is instead old-style printf formatting.

title: Bitwise AND / set intersection
short: Combines two integers bit by bit (1 only where both bits are 1), or intersects two sets.
long: Often used with a bit mask to keep selected bits: flags & MASK.

title: Bitwise OR / set union / type union
short: ORs two integers bit by bit, unions two sets, or forms a union type like int | None.
long: The type-union meaning (PEP 604) works in annotations and, since 3.10, at runtime for isinstance.

title: Bitwise XOR / symmetric difference
short: Sets each result bit where exactly one operand's bit is 1; for sets, the elements in one but not both.
long: x ^ x is 0, which makes it handy for toggling bits and simple parity checks.

title: Bitwise NOT
short: Flips every bit of an integer; because of two's complement, ~n equals -(n + 1).
long: Occasionally used as a 'from the other end' index trick: seq[~i] is seq[-i-1].

title: Left shift
short: Shifts an integer's bits left by n places, which multiplies it by 2 ** n.
long: Used to build masks (1 << bit) and to pack fields into a single integer.

title: Right shift
short: Shifts an integer's bits right by n places, an efficient floor-divide by 2 ** n.
long: For non-negative numbers it simply drops the low bits.

title: Less-than
short: True when the left value orders before the right; also proper-subset for sets.
long: Comparisons chain: a < b < c means a < b and b < c, with b evaluated once.

title: Greater-than
short: True when the left value orders after the right; also proper-superset for sets.
long: Mixing unorderable types (str and int) raises TypeError rather than guessing.

title: Less-than-or-equal
short: True when the left value is smaller than or equal to the right; subset for sets.
long: Reads as one operator, so no space between < and =.

title: Greater-than-or-equal
short: True when the left value is larger than or equal to the right; superset for sets.

title: Equality test
short: Compares values for equality and returns a bool; it does not assign.
long: Different from is, which checks identity. Custom classes control == through __eq__; without one, it falls back to identity.

title: Inequality test
short: True when the two values are not equal; the negation of ==.

title: Add-and-assign
short: Adds the right side to the current value of the left and rebinds the name to the result.
long: For mutable objects like lists it updates in place (calls __iadd__); for immutables like ints and strings it builds a new object and rebinds.

title: Subtract-and-assign
short: Subtracts the right side from the left and stores the result back in the same name.

title: Multiply-and-assign
short: Multiplies the left value by the right and rebinds the name to the product.

title: Divide-and-assign
short: Divides the left value by the right (true division, float result) and rebinds the name.

title: Floor-divide-and-assign
short: Floor-divides the left value by the right and stores the whole-number result back.

title: Modulo-and-assign
short: Replaces the left value with its remainder when divided by the right.

title: Power-and-assign
short: Raises the left value to the power of the right and rebinds the name.

title: AND-and-assign
short: Bitwise-ANDs the left value with the right (or intersects sets) and stores it back.

title: OR-and-assign
short: Bitwise-ORs the left value with the right, unions sets, or updates a dict in place.

title: XOR-and-assign
short: Bitwise-XORs the left value with the right (or symmetric-difference for sets) and rebinds it.

title: Left-shift-and-assign
short: Shifts the left value's bits left by the right amount and stores the result back.

title: Right-shift-and-assign
short: Shifts the left value's bits right by the right amount and rebinds the name.

title: Matmul-and-assign
short: Matrix-multiplies the left operand by the right in place; meaningful for array libraries.

title: Logical AND
short: True only if both sides are truthy; short-circuits and returns the first falsy operand, else the last.
long: The right side is not evaluated when the left is already falsy. Because it returns an operand (not a strict bool), x and default is a common guard.

title: Logical OR
short: True if either side is truthy; short-circuits and returns the first truthy operand, else the last.
long: value or fallback supplies a default when value is empty, 0, None, or False.

title: Logical NOT
short: Inverts truthiness, always returning a real bool.
long: Lower precedence than comparisons, so not a == b is not (a == b). Also pairs with in and is: not in, is not.

title: Membership test
short: True when the left value is found in the container on the right.
long: For dicts it checks keys; for strings it checks substrings. Efficient for sets and dicts, linear for lists.

title: for ... in iterable
short: Separates the loop variable(s) from the iterable a for loop or comprehension draws from.
long: The iterable is asked for an iterator once; each pass binds the next item to the loop target.

title: Identity test
short: True only when both sides are the exact same object in memory, not merely equal.
long: Use it for singletons — is None, is True — and use == for value comparison. Small ints and interned strings may share identity as an implementation detail; do not rely on it.

title: if statement
short: Runs the indented block below only when its condition is truthy.
long: Optionally followed by elif and else clauses; the first matching branch runs and the rest are skipped.

title: Conditional expression
short: In A if cond else B, chooses between two values inline without a full if block.
long: The condition is evaluated first; only the chosen side is then evaluated. It is an expression, so it can sit inside a call or a list.

title: Comprehension filter
short: Keeps only the items for which the following condition is true.
long: Placed after the for clause. With no else it filters; an if...else before the for is a conditional expression on the output instead.
example: [n for n in xs if n > 0]

title: elif clause
short: Tests another condition when all preceding if/elif conditions were false.
long: Short for 'else if' but without the extra nesting. Only the first true branch in the chain runs.

title: else clause
short: The fallback block that runs when the if/elif chain found no true condition.
long: Also legal after for and while (runs if the loop was not broken out of) and after try (runs if no exception occurred).

title: for loop
short: Iterates over each item of an iterable, running the indented body once per item.
long: Python's for is a for-each; there is no manual counter. Use enumerate() for an index, range() for a count. A trailing else runs only if the loop finished without break.

title: while loop
short: Repeats the indented body as long as its condition stays truthy, checking before each pass.
long: Best when the number of iterations is not known up front. Make sure something inside the body can eventually make the condition false, or add a break.

title: break
short: Immediately exits the innermost for or while loop, skipping any loop else clause.
long: Only the one enclosing loop is left; outer loops keep running. To leave several at once, refactor into a function and return.

title: continue
short: Skips the rest of the current loop iteration and jumps to the next one.
long: The loop condition (while) or the next item (for) is evaluated as usual. Handy for skipping items that fail an early check.

title: pass
short: A statement that does nothing, used where syntax requires a body but you have no code yet.
long: Common in stub classes and empty except blocks. Unlike a comment, it is a real statement the parser accepts as the whole body.

title: return
short: Ends the current function call and hands a value back to whoever called it.
long: return with no expression (or falling off the end of the function) returns None. Only valid inside a function.

title: yield
short: Produces one value from a generator and pauses the function until the next value is requested.
long: Any def containing yield is a generator function: calling it returns a generator object and runs no body until iterated. Local state is preserved between yields. yield from delegates to another iterable.

title: function definition
short: Defines a named function: binds the name to a function object whose body is the indented block.
long: The body does not run now — only when the function is later called. Parameters are listed in the parentheses; a docstring may be the first line of the body.

title: class definition
short: Defines a new type: a template for objects that bundle data and the methods acting on it.
long: The indented block runs once to build the class body; methods take self as their first parameter. Any base classes go in parentheses after the name.

title: lambda expression
short: Creates a small anonymous function in a single expression: lambda params: result.
long: It has no name, no statements, and no annotations — just one expression that becomes the return value. Best for short callbacks like sort keys; name it with def if it grows.

title: global declaration
short: Tells a function that the listed names refer to module-level variables, so assignments update those.
long: Without it, assigning to a name inside a function creates a new local. Reading a global needs no declaration. Overuse of global makes code hard to follow.

title: nonlocal declaration
short: Binds a name to a variable in the nearest enclosing function, letting an inner function reassign it.
long: Used in closures where an inner function needs to update state owned by the outer function rather than a global.

title: import statement
short: Loads another module and binds a name to it so its contents can be used.
long: The module runs once on first import and is then cached. Plain import mod keeps the mod. prefix; from mod import name pulls a single object into the current namespace.

title: from ... import ...
short: Imports specific names out of a module directly into the current namespace.
long: from pkg import mod can also pull a submodule. A leading dot (from . import x) means a relative import within the same package.

title: as (alias)
short: Gives an imported name, a with-context, or a caught exception a local name of your choosing.
long: import numpy as np renames on import; except ValueError as e binds the exception; with open(p) as f binds the context manager's result.

title: with statement
short: Runs a block with a context manager that is guaranteed to be cleaned up on exit.
long: The manager's setup runs on entry and its teardown runs on the way out, even if an exception is raised — closing files, releasing locks, ending transactions. Several managers can be comma-separated.

title: try block
short: Marks code whose exceptions should be caught by the except clauses that follow.
long: Optional else runs when no exception was raised; finally always runs last for cleanup. Keep the protected block small so you catch only what you mean to.

title: except clause
short: Handles a matching exception raised in the try block.
long: except SomeError as e binds the exception object. A bare except: catches almost everything and is discouraged. Clauses are tried top to bottom; the first match wins.

title: finally clause
short: A block that always runs when leaving the try — normally, via exception, or via return.
long: Use it for cleanup that must happen no matter what. A return or raise inside finally will override one from the try body.

title: raise
short: Throws an exception, unwinding the call stack until something catches it.
long: raise Err("msg") creates and throws; a bare raise inside an except re-throws the current one. raise X from Y records a cause for the traceback.

title: assert
short: Raises AssertionError if the condition is false; an optional message follows a comma.
long: A sanity check for 'this should never happen', not for validating user input — assertions are stripped when Python runs with -O.

title: del statement
short: Unbinds a name, or removes an item/slice/attribute from a container.
long: del x removes the name from the namespace; del d[key] deletes a mapping entry; del lst[1:3] removes a slice. It does not force the object to be freed if other references remain.

title: async def / async for / async with
short: Marks a coroutine or an async iteration/context that an event loop can suspend and resume.
long: Calling an async def returns a coroutine that does nothing until awaited or scheduled on a loop. async for and async with work with asynchronous iterables and context managers.

title: await
short: Pauses the current coroutine until the awaited awaitable completes, yielding control to the event loop.
long: Only valid inside an async def. While one coroutine is paused here, the loop can run others, which is where the concurrency comes from.

title: True
short: The boolean true value; also equal to the integer 1.
long: A keyword, so it cannot be reassigned. Comparisons and truthiness checks return this or False.

title: False
short: The boolean false value; also equal to the integer 0.
long: One of several falsy values, alongside None, 0, "", [], {}. A keyword and cannot be reassigned.

title: None
short: The single 'no value' object, returned by functions that do not return anything else.
long: Test for it with is None. Commonly used as a default parameter value that the function then replaces with a fresh object.

title: String literal
short: A run of text; single and double quotes are interchangeable in Python.
long: Backslash starts an escape (\n, \t, \"). Adjacent string literals with only whitespace between them are automatically concatenated.

title: f-string (formatted literal)
short: A string whose { } fields hold expressions that are evaluated and inserted when the line runs.
long: Add :spec for formatting (f"{x:.2f}") and ={ } to show both the expression and its value (f"{x=}"). Double a brace to print it literally.

title: raw string
short: A string where backslashes are literal, so escape sequences are not processed.
long: Ideal for regular expressions and Windows paths: r"\d+" is a backslash then d, not a control character. It still cannot end with a lone backslash.

title: bytes literal
short: A sequence of raw bytes (values 0-255) rather than text.
long: Used for binary data and for I/O that has not been decoded to str yet. Indexing a bytes gives an int; slicing gives bytes.

title: triple-quoted string
short: A string that may span multiple lines and contain unescaped single quotes.
long: As the first statement of a module, class, or function it becomes the docstring. Line breaks inside it are part of the text.

title: integer literal
short: A whole number with unlimited precision — no overflow, no fixed width.
long: Digits may be grouped with underscores for readability (1_000_000). A leading zero on a non-zero number is a syntax error; use 0o for octal.

title: floating-point literal
short: A number with a decimal point or exponent, stored as a 64-bit IEEE-754 double.
long: Only approximate: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Compare with math.isclose, and use decimal.Decimal for money.

title: scientific notation
short: The e (or E) marks a power-of-ten exponent: 1e3 is 1000.0, 2.5e-4 is 0.00025.
long: Any literal with an exponent is a float, even 1e0. The exponent must be an integer and may be signed.

title: hexadecimal literal
short: Base-16 integer; digits 0-9 and a-f, prefix 0x.
long: Compact for bit masks, colours, and byte values. 0xFF is 255. Case of the digits and the x does not matter.

title: octal literal
short: Base-8 integer with prefix 0o; each digit is three bits.
long: Mostly seen for Unix file permission bits, e.g. 0o755.

title: binary literal
short: Base-2 integer with prefix 0b, written directly as bits.
long: Useful for spelling out flags and masks. Underscores can group nibbles: 0b1010_0001.

title: digit separator
short: An underscore between digits that is ignored by Python and only aids reading.
long: Allowed in any numeric base. It may not lead, trail, or be doubled: 1_000 is fine, _1000 and 1__000 are not.

title: imaginary literal
short: A trailing j (or J) makes the number the imaginary part of a complex value.
long: 3+4j is a complex number; access .real and .imag, or use cmath for complex math.

title: comment
short: Everything from the # to the end of the line is ignored by Python.
long: There is no block-comment syntax; each line needs its own #. A # as the very first line with ! (a shebang) tells the OS which interpreter to run.

title: explicit line continuation
short: A backslash as the last character of a line joins it with the next physical line.
long: Only needed outside brackets — code already inside (), [], or {} continues automatically, which is the preferred style. Nothing, not even a space, may follow the backslash.

title: indentation increase
short: Leading whitespace that starts a new nested block; indentation is syntax in Python, not just style.
long: The amount must be consistent within a block. Mixing tabs and spaces for the same block is an error. Four spaces per level is the convention.

title: indentation decrease
short: A drop back to a previous indentation level, which closes one or more nested blocks.
long: The new indentation must line up exactly with an enclosing block, or Python raises an IndentationError.

title: logical line end
short: The end of a statement — the point where one instruction finishes and the next begins.
long: Distinct from a blank line or a line break inside brackets, which the tokenizer treats as insignificant.

title: non-logical newline
short: A line break that does not end a statement — a blank line, or a wrap inside ()/[]/{}.
long: The tokenizer emits it so tools can reproduce formatting, but it has no effect on program meaning.

title: Keyword-only marker
short: A bare * in a parameter list: every parameter after it must be passed by name, never positionally.
long: It carries no name of its own. Callers then have to write func(..., flag=True) rather than relying on argument order, which keeps call sites readable.

title: Identifier
short: A name your code chose — a variable, function, class, module, or attribute.
long: Not a keyword, so you are free to (re)bind it. Python resolves it by scope: local, then enclosing function, then module global, then built-ins.

title: Name being defined
short: This identifier is the name a def or class statement is creating.
long: After this line the name is bound in the surrounding scope and can be referred to elsewhere.

title: Parameter name
short: A local name that will hold one of the arguments passed when the function is called.
long: It exists only inside the function body. A following : gives it a type hint and a following = gives it a default.

title: Attribute name
short: The name looked up on the object to the left of the dot.
long: Python searches the instance, then its class, then base classes. If a ( follows, the attribute found is then called.

title: Name being called
short: The function, method, or class that the parentheses just after it will invoke.
long: The name only refers to the callable; it is the following () that runs it.

title: Operator or punctuation
short: A symbol that combines values or marks the structure of the code.
long: CodeCrawler could not pin down a more specific meaning here — often because the surrounding file does not fully parse. Press the ask key for a precise explanation.

title: String literal
short: A piece of text embedded directly in the source.
long: Quote style and prefix (f, r, b) change how it is interpreted. Adjacent literals are auto-joined.

title: Numeric literal
short: A number written directly in the source — integer, float, or complex.
long: The form (0x, 0o, 0b, a decimal point, a trailing j) determines the type and base.

title: Token
short: A single unit of Python source with no database entry yet.
long: Press the ask key to get an explanation, then save it so it is here next time.
